result.target_topic: Policy for changing loan classification between HFI and HFS
result.target_summary: Changes in loan classification from held-for-investment (HFI) to held-for-sale (HFS) or vice versa require a demonstrated change in management's intent and ability. Transfers from HFI to HFS involve reversing the allowance for credit losses through earnings, potentially recording direct write-offs for credit deterioration, or establishing an HFS valuation allowance.

target_year_over_year_context.explanation:
Both disclosures describe the cash flow classification for held-for-investment loans (investing activities) and the treatment when reclassified to held-for-sale (cash flows remain in investing activities).

Both disclosures address the accounting treatment for changes in loan classification between held-for-investment (HFI) and held-for-sale (HFS). The 2023 disclosure establishes the reclassification mechanics when intent changes, and the 2024 disclosure expands on this by specifying the required demonstrated change in intent and ability, along with the specific allowance reversal and valuation allowance treatments for HFI-to-HFS transfers. They cover the same specific subject: the accounting mechanics of loan classification changes.

comparisons.peer_summary: Loans include held for investment loans accounted for at amortized cost (net of allowance or fair value option) and held for sale loans at lower of cost or fair value. Interest is recognized on an accrual basis over the life of the loan.
comparisons.comparison: Both C and GS disclose the fundamental classification and valuation basis for loans held for investment (HFI) versus loans held for sale (HFS). C specifies that HFI loans are held based on management intent and that transfers to HFS involve credit loss reversal and potential direct write-offs. GS similarly defines HFI loans as accounted for at amortized cost and HFS loans at the lower of cost or fair value, confirming the same structural distinction in how these loan categories are valued and reported.

sentences.text: Changes to the initial classification of a loan should be made only when there is a demonstrated change in management's intent and ability (i.e., management now has the intent and ability to sell the loan when it had previously intended to hold the loan for the foreseeable future or vice versa).
If a loan changes its classification from HFI to HFS, the related allowance for credit losses is reversed in earnings through the Provision for credit losses.

Loans includes (i) loans held for investment that are accounted for at amortized cost net of allowance for loan losses or at fair value under the fair value option and (ii) loans held for sale that are accounted for at the lower of cost or fair value.

comparisons.peer_topic: Loan portfolio transfer and loss recognition policies
comparisons.peer_summary: Loans transferred from held-for-investment to held-for-sale are recorded at the lower of cost or fair value, while subsequent retention involves transfer to held-for-investment at amortized cost and impairment assessment. Credit-related losses are charged against the allowance for loan losses, whereas non-credit losses are recognized in noninterest revenue.
comparisons.comparison: JPM provides the most detailed comparable policy to C regarding the mechanics of HFI to HFS transfers. Both companies state that loans moved from HFI to HFS are valued at the lower of cost or fair value. C specifies that credit deterioration triggers a direct write-off of the amortized cost basis and reverses the allowance. JPM aligns with this by stating credit-related losses are charged against the allowance for loan losses upon transfer. Both also cover the reverse scenario: C notes HFS to HFI transfers at amortized cost with new ACL assessment, and JPM confirms retention of HFS loans transfers them back to HFI at amortized cost for impairment assessment.

sentences.text: If a loan changes its classification from HFI to HFS, the related allowance for credit losses is reversed in earnings through the Provision for credit losses.

Also, if the loan's fair value is lower than the loan's amortized cost basis due to credit deterioration, the initial downward difference is recorded as a direct write-off of the loan's amortized cost basis through gross credit losses, which establishes the new cost basis of the loan immediately prior to transfer to HFS for purposes of applying the lower of cost or market value.
On the other hand, if a loan changes its classification from HFS to HFI, any HFS valuation allowance is reversed through Other revenue.
The loan is transferred to HFI at its amortized cost basis and assessed for an allowance for credit losses.
Loans in the held-for-investment portfolio that management decides to sell are transferred to the held-for-sale portfolio at the lower of cost or fair value on the date of transfer.

Credit-related losses are charged against the allowance for loan losses; non-credit related losses such as those due to changes in interest rates or foreign currency exchange rates are recognized in noninterest revenue.
In the event that management decides to retain a loan in the held-for-sale portfolio, the loan is transferred to the held-for-investment portfolio at amortized cost on the date of transfer.
These loans are subsequently assessed for impairment based on the Firm's allowance methodology.

comparisons.peer_topic: Impairment Recognition for AFS Securities Intent to Sell
comparisons.peer_summary: If management intends to sell an AFS security or it is more likely than not they will be required to sell before recovery of the amortized cost basis, the entire unrealized loss is recognized in Other revenues and the amortized cost basis is written down to fair value. Any previously established allowance for credit losses (ACL) is written off in this scenario.
comparisons.comparison: While MS disclosure focuses on AFS debt securities rather than loans, it mirrors the 'intent to sell' valuation logic described by C. C states that HFI to HFS transfers require a demonstrated change in management intent and involve writing down to fair value (lower of cost or market). MS describes the same 'intent to sell' trigger for AFS securities, where the entire unrealized loss is recognized in earnings and the basis is written down to fair value, reflecting a consistent accounting philosophy regarding the recognition of losses when management intent shifts to selling.

sentences.text: Changes to the initial classification of a loan should be made only when there is a demonstrated change in management's intent and ability (i.e., management now has the intent and ability to sell the loan when it had previously intended to hold the loan for the foreseeable future or vice versa).

Also, if the loan's fair value is lower than the loan's amortized cost basis due to credit deterioration, the initial downward difference is recorded as a direct write-off of the loan's amortized cost basis through gross credit losses, which establishes the new cost basis of the loan immediately prior to transfer to HFS for purposes of applying the lower of cost or market value.

AFS securities in an unrealized loss position are first evaluated to determine whether there is an intent to sell or it is more likely than not the Firm will be required to sell before recovery of the amortized cost basis.

If so, the amortized cost basis is written down to the fair value of the security such that the entire unrealized loss is recognized in Other revenues, and any previously established ACL is written off.
